'''Xiaoxing Xi''' ({{lang-zh|c={{linktext|郗|小|星}}|p=Xī Xiǎoxīng}}; born 1957) is a Chinese-born American materials physicist specializing in the electromagnetic properties of thin films. He is the [[Laura H. Carnell]] Professor and former chair at the Physics Department of [[Temple University]] in [[Philadelphia]].<ref name=temple>{{cite web |url=https://phys.cst.temple.edu/xiaoxing-xi.html |title=Xiaoxing Xi |publisher=Temple University |access-date=14 September 2015 |archive-date=27 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150927194822/https://phys.cst.temple.edu/xiaoxing-xi.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> In May 2015, the [[United States Department of Justice]] arrested him on charges of having sent restricted American technology to China. All charges against him were dropped in September 2015.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/the-two-asian-americas |title=The Two Asian Americas |date=21 October 2015 |newspaper=The New Yorker}}</ref>

{{anchor|History|Biography}}

==Career==
Xi was born in China and grew up during the [[Cultural Revolution]]. He matriculated to the physics department at [[Peking University]] in 1978 as part of the first class following the Cultural Revolution. He graduated with a BSc in physics in 1982.<ref name="temple" /> He studied under [[Weiyan Guan]], and received his PhD in 1987 for work in superconductivity.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Feder |first=Toni |date=2025-06-20 |title=Q&A: Xiaoxing Xi on the wrongful arrest that upended his research and his life |journal=[[Physics Today]] |volume=78 |issue=8 |pages=21–24 |language=English |doi=10.1063/pt.klzb.kikk|bibcode=2025PhT..2025f4388F |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Following graduate studies, Xi was a researcher at the [[Karlsruhe Institute of Technology#Campus Nord|Karlsruhe Nuclear Research Center]] in Germany, where he worked on epitaxial [[yttrium barium copper oxide]] thin films. Thirumalai Venkatesan visited Karlsruhe and made offers to both Xi and his wife, who is also a physicist, to come work with him at Bell Communication Research at [[Rutgers University]]. Xi and his wife accepted Venkatesan's offer and moved to the United States in 1989. When Venkatesan moved to the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]] five years later, Xi and his wife moved as well.<ref name=":0" /> While at Maryland Xi researched high-temperature superconductor field-effect transistors.<ref name=":0" />

In 1995 Xi's wife received an offer from [[Pennsylvania State University]] and Xi received an offer as the [[spousal hire]]. There Xi shifted his research to ultrathin ferromagnetic films.<ref name=":0" /> Xi's wife is still a physics professor at Pennsylvania State University.<ref>{{cite news |date=14 September 2015 |script-title=zh:美国之音中文部专访著名华裔学者郗小星 |trans-title=VOA Chinese interviews famous scholar Xiaoxing Xi |url=http://www.voachinese.com/content/voa-chinese-interview-xi-xiaoxing-temple-physicist/2962658.html |newspaper=Voice of America |language=zh}}</ref> While at Pennsylvania State University, Xi was nominated as a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] by the Division of Materials Physics "for his extensive and seminal contributions to the science and applications of thin film materials including high temperature superconductors, ferroelectrics, and magnesium diboride."<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Division of Materials Physics |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/aps-fellowship/dmp-fellowship |access-date=2025-09-01 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref>

In 2009 Xi became a professor at [[Temple University]]. Xi was named chairman of Temple University's physics department in 2014.<ref name="temple" />

Xi has naturalized as a US citizen.<ref name="apuzzo">{{cite news |author=Matt Apuzzo |date=11 September 2015 |title=U.S. Drops Charges That Professor Shared Technology With China |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/12/us/politics/us-drops-charges-that-professor-shared-technology-with-china.html |newspaper=The New York Times}}</ref><ref name="voa">{{cite news |date=14 September 2015 |title=Chinese-born Professor Faults US Authorities for Arrest |url=https://www.voanews.com/a/feds-to-drop-fraud-charges-against-chinese-born-us-professor/2962631.html |newspaper=Voice of America}}</ref> He and his wife have two daughters and live in suburban Philadelphia.<ref name="apuzzo" />

==False accusation of spying==
In 2015, police raided Xi's home and arrested him at gunpoint in front of his wife and two daughters. The US Justice Department (DOJ) had accused the scientist of illegally sending trade secrets to China: specifically, the design of a [[Rotating pocket heater|pocket heater]] used in [[superconductor]] research. Xi was indicted on four counts of wire fraud, putting him under threat of 80 years in prison and $1 million in fines.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Conover |first=Emily |date=October 2015 |title=Charges Dropped for Physicist Accused of Sharing Sensitive Technology with China |url=https://www.aps.org/archives/publications/apsnews/201510/charges-dropped.cfm |access-date=2025-09-01 |website=www.aps.org |publisher=American Physical Society |language=en}}</ref> Xi's daughter Joyce Xi said, "newscasters surrounded our home and tried to film through windows. The FBI rummaged through all our belongings and carried off electronics and documents containing many private details of our lives. For months, we lived in fear of FBI intimidation and surveillance. We worried about our safety in public, given that my dad's face was plastered all over the news. My dad was unable to work, and his reputation was shattered."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/voices/2021/04/27/chinese-american-professor-bias-fbi-attacks-government-column/7385996002/|title = The FBI wrongly accused my father of spying for China. Government has a role in anti-Asian violence|website = [[USA Today]]}}</ref>

Temple University forced Xi to take administrative leave and suspended him as chair of the Physics Department. He was also banned from accessing his lab or communicating with his students directly. It was later learned that FBI agents had been listening to his phone calls and reading his emails for months — possibly years.<ref name="ACLU-Battling">{{Cite web |first1=Patrick |last1=Toomey |first2=Ashley |last2=Gorski |url=https://www.aclu.org/news/national-security/a-chinese-american-scientist-and-his-family-are-battling-the-fbis-profiling-in-court/|title=A Chinese American Scientist and His Family Are Battling the FBI's Profiling in Court |website=ACLU News & Commentary |date=2 April 2021}}</ref>

In September 2015, however, the DOJ dropped all charges against him after leading scientists, including a co-inventor of the pocket heater, provided [[affidavit]]s that the schematics that Xi shared with Chinese scientists were not for a pocket heater or other restricted technology.<ref name=apuzzo/><ref name=voa/> According to Xi's lawyer Peter Zeidenberg, the government did not understand the complicated science and failed to consult with experts before arresting him.<ref name=apuzzo/> He said that the information Xi shared as part of "typical academic collaboration" was about a different device, which Xi co-invented and which is not restricted technology.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2015/sep/12/charges-withdrawn-against-professor-accused-of-stealing-us-secrets-for-china |title=Charges withdrawn against professor accused of stealing US secrets for China |date=12 September 2015 |newspaper=The Guardian}}</ref>

In 2017 Xi filed a lawsuit suing the United States and the FBI agents over violations of fourth and fifth amendment rights. Xi is being represented in part by the [[American Civil Liberties Union]]. The suit alleges that Xi was surveilled without a warrant and the FBI knowingly made false claims.<ref name="ACLU-Battling"/><ref name="ACLU-XIvUS">{{Cite web |title=Xi v. United States – Challenge to Warrantless Surveillance |url=https://www.aclu.org/cases/xi-v-united-states-challenge-warrantless-surveillance |access-date=2022-09-15 |website=American Civil Liberties Union |language=en}}</ref>
In 2021, Xi a Philadelphia court rejected his legal claims for damages. The judge ruled that the claims involved matters of discretion and judgement of the defendants.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/lawsuits-immigration-philadelphia-arrests-china-35af848dd11d999dd045654d0f0e7ce0|title = US judge tosses claims by Chinese-born professor over arrest|website = [[Associated Press]]|date = 20 April 2021}}</ref> Xi's appeal was argued in September, 2022, and was allowed to move forward in May 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-25 |title=After being wrongfully accused of spying for China, prof wins appeal to sue government |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/asian-america/wrongfully-accused-spying-china-professor-wins-appeal-sue-government-rcna86109 |access-date=2025-09-01 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref> However, recent Supreme Court decisions may make it difficult to obtain damages for violations of constitutional rights.<ref name="WHYY-2022-09-14">{{Cite news |last=Yu |first=Alan |date=September 14, 2022 |title=Temple professor continues legal journey to sue FBI for wrongful prosecution |url=https://whyy.org/articles/temple-professor-suing-fbi-for-wrongful-prosecution-expected-in-court/ |access-date=2022-09-15 |work=WHYY |language=en-US}}</ref> 

In 2020 Xi was awarded the [[Andrei Sakharov Prize (APS)|Andrei Sakharov Prize]] of the [[American Physical Society]] "For articulate and steadfast advocacy in support of the US scientific community and open scientific exchange, and especially his efforts to clarify the nature of international scientific collaboration in cases involving allegations of scientific espionage."<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Andrei Sakharov Prize |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/prize/andrei-sakharov |access-date=2025-09-01 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Selected works==
Xiaoxing Xi has published more than 300 research papers and holds three patents. His research focus is on [[materials physics]], specifically the applications of [[epitaxial]] thin films and nanoscale heterostructures. His key publications include:<ref name=temple/>
